Inventory Costing Methods Explained: LIFO, FIFO, and Weighted Average Inventory costing is
an important concept in accounting that every business student needs to understand.

Therefore, inventory valuation methods are used to figure out the cost inventory has and
it also has a significant impact on the valuation of ending inventory, cost of goods sold,
and gross profit on the income statement.

So today, I am going to share with you the three
most common inventory costing methods — LIFO, FIFO, and Weighted Average.

But before
heading toward costing methods, there are some basics to be clarified about inventory
costing.
So, What is Inventory Costing?

in the First Place Inventory costing refers to the
method a company uses to assign costs to the units held in inventory. Since inventory is
purchased at different times and different prices, the costing method determines which
costs are matched with revenues to calculate cost of goods sold and gross margin.

Why Does
Inventory Costing even Matter?

The selected inventory costing method impacts directly to
the balance sheet and income statement.

It determines the value of inventory assets and
also affects the calculation of cost of goods sold and gross profit for the period.

This
in turn impacts net income and taxation.

The Three Main Inventory Costing Methods There
are three primary costing methods used for periodic and perpetual inventory systems: 1.

FIFO: First-In, First-Out The FIFO inventory valuation method assumes that the oldest
inventory units purchased are sold first.

Inventory value reflects the costs of the most
recent purchases.
Cost of goods sold is calculated using costs of the oldest units.
Results in higher net income and higher inventory asset value.

LIFO: Last-In, First-Out
The LIFO method assumes that the most recent inventory purchases are sold first.

Inventory
value reflects the costs of the oldest purchases.

Cost of goods sold uses costs of most
recent purchases.
Results in lower net income and lower inventory asset value.

Weighted
Average Cost The weighted average cost method averages the cost of units available for
sale.

Inventory value and cost of goods sold are based on the weighted average cost per
unit.
Results in moderate net income and inventory valuation.

When to Use Each Inventory
Costing Method FIFO is simple to apply and matches current revenues with oldest costs.

It
is commonly used by retailers.
LIFO better matches current revenues with current costs.

It
is utilized to reduce taxable income.

Weighted average is easy to understand and smooths
out fluctuations in inventory costing.

Example LIFO Inventory Costing Problem Let’s apply
the LIFO method to solve an inventory costing problem. Rana Furniture Factory had the
following lumber inventory transactions in June: June 1: Beginning inventory of 5 units at
$16 per unit June 5: Purchased 13 units at $20 per unit June 19: Sold 9 units June 23:
Purchased 8 units at $18 per unit June 30: Sold 12 units Determine the ending cost of
inventory on June 30 using the LIFO perpetual inventory method. Solution: Beginning
inventory on June 1 = 5 units at $16 per unit = $80 Purchase on June 5 of 13 units at $20
per unit = $260 Sale on June 19 of 9 units removed from latest purchase: 9 units removed
at $20 per unit = $180 Remaining inventory is 13–9 = 4 units at $20 per unit = $80
Purchase on June 23 of 8 units at $18 per unit = $144 Total inventory = 4 units at $20 per
unit + 8 units at $18 per unit = $80 + $144 = $224 Sale on June 30 of 12 units removed the
latest 8 units at $18 and 4 units at $20 8 units removed at $18 per unit = $144 4 units
removed at $20 per unit = $80 Remaining inventory is 0 units Ending inventory on June 30
is 0 units Using the LIFO perpetual method demonstrates the flow of inventory costs and
allows us to arrive at the accurate ending inventory valuation.
